summary: FireWatch is a web app for the NASA hackathon challenge “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots”. It pulls active-fire detections from NASA FIRMS (MODIS on Terra/Aqua, VIIRS on NOAA-20/21) through a Node.js/Express backend with DuckDB, caching every fetched day so nothing is downloaded twice. Hotspots are harmonized by matching detections across sensors and calibrating counts per area. Users draw any area of interest on a React/Leaflet map and see a burning activity calendar, climatology, anomaly flags and critical fire periods, with all times converted from UTC to local time. It supports early warning, emergency response, science and land management.
details:
FireWatch is a web application that turns NASA FIRMS active-fire detections into a burning activity calendar for any area of interest on Earth. A user draws an area on the map, and the app shows each day’s fire activity across several years as a calendar heatmap. It also shows a climatology (what is normal for each time of year), flags unusual days, and lists critical periods such as season start, peak week and the most intense days.

MODIS (1 km pixels) and VIIRS (375 m pixels) detect the same fires differently, so adding their hotspot counts directly would be misleading. FireWatch harmonizes them in two ways:

  • Hotspot level: MODIS and VIIRS detections are matched by location and time, and each hotspot is labelled as seen by both sensors or by only one.
  • Calendar level: detections are converted into burning grid-cell-days, so one fire counts once no matter how many hotspots it produces. A per-area calibration factor then expresses VIIRS in MODIS-equivalent terms.

All timestamps are stored in UTC. The calendar days are shown in the area’s local time (or the user’s device time), so a night-time satellite pass lands on the correct local date. Every day of data we fetch is saved in a local cache, so the same request never downloads the same data twice.

What benefits does it have?

  • Fire history stays comparable even though the satellites and their detection sensitivity differ.
  • Users can see how an area’s current season compares with its own historical baseline.
  • A sensor timeline and a “consistent” mode make it visible when an apparent increase is caused by an added satellite rather than by more fire.
  • The cache reduces repeated downloads and keeps us within the FIRMS API rate limit.
  • A methodology panel explains the assumptions, so non-experts can judge how far to trust the numbers.

What is the intended impact?

We want to help early-warning teams, emergency responders, scientists and land managers spot unusual fire conditions and critical periods, using a record that stays consistent across sensors. This matters especially as MODIS approaches the end of its mission and VIIRS takes over the long-term record.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

  • Data: NASA FIRMS Area API (MODIS on Terra/Aqua, VIIRS on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21)
  • Backend: Node.js, Express, DuckDB, Luxon and geo-tz for time zones
  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet (OpenStreetMap basemap), Recharts
  • Development: Antigravity IDE with Gemini, plus Claude for planning, debugging and code review [confirm your team’s AI-use disclosure and edit this line]
  • Hardware: standard Windows laptops, no special hardware

How is it creative?

  • The calendar is the main interface, instead of the usual map of dots. It shows fire seasons across years at a glance.
  • A sensor timeline sits beside the calendar and explains why counts can step up when a satellite joins.
  • A union mode and a consistent mode let users choose between maximum detection and trend stability.
  • The calibration factor is computed separately for each area, because fire regimes differ between regions.
  • Calendar days follow local time instead of UTC.
  • Data is fetched lazily and cached, so any area on Earth can be explored without downloading the planet.
  • [Add only if you integrate it before submitting: we also measure how many grid cells are seen by both sensors and by only one, at several resolutions, with a by-chance baseline.]

What factors did your team consider?

  • Sensor differences: pixel size, overpass times and the NOAA-21 start, which can create artificial steps in the series.
  • Honesty about uncertainty: the calibration is an approximation, so we label it as a MODIS-equivalent estimate and document it.
  • Data volume and limits: the FIRMS API rate limit, large downloads and the five-day request window.
  • Time zones: local days for correct calendars, with a fallback for open-sea areas that have no time zone.
  • Quality: low-confidence detections are filtered by default, and the user can switch this off.
  • Security and reproducibility: the API key stays on the server, and results are cached.
